title: Triangulene-based diradicals as a blueprint for molecular quantum platforms with optical addressability and long spin coherence times
authors: Arup Sarkar, Cathal Hogan, Conor Ryan, Lorenzo A. Mariano, Alessandro Lunghi
abstract: The identification of molecules that combine long spin coherence times and efficient spin-optical interfaces, ideally at room temperature, is pivotal towards the development of molecular quantum technology. By means of advanced first-principles methods, we here unravel the electronic structure for triangulene (1), its aza-cation derivative (2), and the crystal of 2,6,10-tri-tert-butyl-4,8,12-trimesityl-triangulene (3), and show that these organic diradicals possess a triplet ground state well separated from the first singlet excited state approaching 0.5 eV, closely resembling solid-state defects like nitrogen vacancy centers. In addition, we compute spin decoherence times due to the interaction with phonons and surrounding nuclear spins, showing that a deuterated molecule of 3 in a nuclear spin-free environment would support $T_2 = 0.21$ ms at 10 K. Importantly, we show that the engineering of specific low-energy vibrations could significantly improve $T_2$ toward the limit imposed by the molecular core spin relaxation, here estimated to be as long as $T_1=27$ ms at 300 K for 2. Finally, we compute two-phonon contributions to inter-system crossing at 300 K for2 as a luminescent prototype, and find that it is highly spin-selective, supporting the possibility to engineer optical read out and spin initialization. These results advance a unified first-principles theoretical foundation of spin decoherence and spin-selective excited-state processes and point to novel chemical design strategies for optically addressable, highly coherent molecular qubits.
summary: The authors propose using triangulene-based diradicals as novel molecular quantum platforms, drawing parallels to robust defects like $	ext{NV}^-$ centers. Using advanced theoretical methods, they calculate spin coherence times and demonstrate that these molecules exhibit optically addressable triplet states suitable for qubit applications. The findings establish a theoretical roadmap for designing highly coherent, room-temperature molecular qubits.
main_problem: The primary goal is developing molecular quantum platforms that combine long spin coherence times with efficient, optically addressable interfaces for quantum computation.
main_result: The study predicts that triangulene-based diradicals possess a triplet ground state resembling $	ext{NV}^-$ centers and can exhibit highly spin-selective optical readouts. Theoretical modeling suggests pathways to achieve long coherence times ($T_2$) approaching the molecular core limit (up to $27 	ext{ ms}$ at $300 	ext{ K}$).
method: The research employs advanced first-principles methods, including multireference quantum chemistry and spin-vibronic coupling calculations. Dynamics are modeled using quantum master equations for phonon and nuclear spin interactions.
model_or_system: The physical systems studied are triangulene (1), its aza-cation derivative (2), and the crystal of 2,6,10-tri-tert-butyl-4,8,12-trimesityl-triangulene (3). The theoretical framework incorporates electronic ($\hat{H}_e$), phonon ($\hat{H}_{ph}$), and electron-phonon coupling ($\hat{H}_{e-ph}$) Hamiltonians.
key_observables: Spin coherence time ($T_2$), spin relaxation time ($T_1$), energy separation between triplet ground state and singlet excited state ($\approx 0.5 	ext{ eV}$), and the rate/selectivity of inter-system crossing (ISC).
important_parameters: $T_2 = 0.21 	ext{ ms}$ at $10 	ext{ K}$; estimated $T_1=27 	ext{ ms}$ at $300 	ext{ K}$; operation ideally at room temperature.
main_assumptions: The calculations rely on expanding the vibronic coupling up to the quadratic term and modeling spin-spin dephasing via fluctuations in the effective magnetic field from nuclear spins.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates $	ext{NV}^-$ center transitions (ISC, IC) alongside molecular representations of Compounds 1, 2, and 3, including the crystal structure of compound 3.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the need for robust molecular qubits, analyzing the electronic structure of triangulene derivatives to show $	ext{NV}^-$ center analogies, calculating spin decoherence from phonons/nuclei, and finally demonstrating optically addressable, spin-selective processes like ISC at room temperature.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the theoretical design principles for solid-state molecular qubits by providing quantitative predictions for coherence times and optical control mechanisms based on first-principles calculations. It bridges fundamental quantum chemistry with applied quantum information science.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematics of electronic processes and triangulene-based diradical structures. a) Schematic representation of the transitions involved in an NV−center’s optical cycle in zero magnetic field. Dashed lines represent ISC and Internal Conversion (IC). Continuous red and blue lines represent spin-preserving photon absorption and emission. States are labelled according to defect’s C3v point-group symmetry. b) Molecular representation of Compounds 1, 2 and 3. c) The experimental crystal structure of compound 3.

FIG. 2. Electronic structure of 1-3. a) Vertical Excitation Energies (VEE) of compounds 1-3a and comparison with the experimental VEE of NV−center in diamond[50, 51]. The degeneracies of the respective triplets/singlets are artificially lifted to aid visualization. b-d) State average canonical orbitals from CASSCF(10,10) calculations for 1-3a. The electronic occupation represents the dominant contribution to the ground-state triplet wavefunction.

FIG. 3. Vibronic coupling for 1-2. Panels a-c) report the decomposition of J and K in atomic and Cartesian contributions. Atom IDs 1-22 correspond to C atoms and 23-34 to H atoms. Values are summed over all possible transitions between any of the three T0,MS states and all other excited states. Blue (orange) histograms report results for 1 (2). Panels d-f) report the value of J and K for different transitions after summing over atomic contributions. Left (right) panels report results for 1 (2).

FIG. 4. Phonons’ density of states and vibronic cou- pling. Panels a-d) report the phonons’ density of states for 1, 2, 3c and 3a, respectively. In each case, the color reports the vibronic coupling between any of the three states T0,MS and any other excited state resolved by phonon frequency.

FIG. 5. Phonons’ density of states and spin-resolved vibronic coupling. Panels a-c) report the phonons’ density of states for 2 color-coded by the intensity of the vibronic coupling between each state T0,MS and the excited state S0.
